vignette:
Presenting Narrative (Session 5)

He arrives exactly on time each week, sits in the same chair by the door, and places his briefcase flat on his knees, both hands resting on top of it. When he speaks, his voice is careful, measured-the same tone he uses during interagency meetings, he once explained. But during the third session, when he described the morning the water came, that voice cracked for a single sentence before he cleared his throat and pressed on.

The flood happened in his home province during the monsoon season fourteen years ago. He was thirty-seven then, working as a mid-level analyst for the Ministry of Planning. The rains had been heavy for a week, but no one expected the river to breach the embankment at night. He remembers the sound first: a low rumble that grew into a roar, then his wife's hand gripping his arm as they climbed onto the roof. They were there for eighteen hours. His mother-in-law, who lived three houses down, did not make it to higher ground. He saw her body floating past at dawn, tangled in a sheet of corrugated iron. He cannot say that word-body-out loud. He says, "I saw her being carried away." Then he stares at the space where the floor meets the wall.

Now, in his current role as a policy analyst for a federal agency in a large North American city, he works on disaster risk reduction frameworks. He chose this job deliberately, he told me. "I thought if I studied the systems, I could make sense of it. I could prevent it from happening to others." But the work has become a double-edged sword. Every time he reviews a floodplain map, his palms sweat. When colleagues present data on climate-related displacement, he feels his chest tighten. He has learned to excuse himself to the restroom, where he splashes cold water on his face and counts backwards from ten until his breathing slows. He has never told anyone at work why those meetings are difficult.

At home, his wife notices the changes. He once loved weekend drives to the countryside; now he refuses to go anywhere near a river, a lake, even a large drainage ditch. He checks the weather forecast obsessively-five, six times a day. If rain is predicted, he becomes irritable, distractible. He has installed three sump pumps in their basement, though they live on a hill. His wife has stopped asking him to explain. They sleep in separate rooms now, because he wakes up drenched in sweat, gasping, convinced he hears water rushing. He never tells her what he dreams about.

He avoids television news during flood season. He skips over online articles about natural disasters, scrolling past them as if they were poisonous. But the images intrude anyway-a flash of brown water in a commercial for laundry detergent, the sound of heavy rain in a movie scene. Each time, his heart hammers, and he feels a wave of nausea so strong he has to sit down. He has learned to hide these reactions behind a blank face.

His PCL-5 score of 55 reflects the severity he tries to suppress. He reported moderate-to-severe difficulty concentrating, especially when deadlines coincide with storm forecasts. He acknowledged feeling detached from others-even his own children, who now live in another city. "I love them," he said, his voice flat. "But it's like there's a pane of glass between me and everyone else." He also admitted to exaggerated startle: the other day, a colleague dropped a binder in the hallway, and he dove under his desk before anyone could see him.

When I asked him what he hopes to get from these sessions, he paused for a long time. "I want to stop being afraid of the sky," he said. Then he added, "But I also need to keep working. The work matters." He straightened his tie, adjusted his briefcase, and waited for the next question.
